tools.name: netobserv_export_flows
tools.description: Exports NetObserv flow records as CSV with the same filters as list_flows. Use when the user needs downloadable flow data for audits or offline analysis.

columns.description: Optional comma-separated column names to include (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace,DstK8S_Namespace,Bytes). Omit to export all columns present in the result.

endTime.description: End of time range as Unix epoch seconds. Defaults to now.

filters.description:
NetObserv filter expression passed to the console plugin (plain text; the client URL-encodes it).

Syntax:
- key=value — exact match; key=a,b — OR multiple values for the same key
- key~pattern — regex / contains match; key!~pattern — NOT regex
- key!=value — not equal; key>number — numeric greater-or-equal (e.g. Bytes>1000)
- AND within a group: & (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace=default&Proto=6)
- OR between groups: | (e.g. SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b)

Prefer the dedicated "namespace" parameter for namespace scope when possible.
Use Kubernetes list tools (namespaces, pods, deployments, etc.) to discover filter values.

Common Kubernetes fields (Src/Dst prefixes mirror each other):
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type (e.g. Pod, Service, Node)
- SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName, SrcK8S_OwnerType, DstK8S_OwnerType (for Deployment, StatefulSet, etc.)
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone, K8S_ClusterName, UDN

Network & flow:
- SrcAddr, DstAddr (IPs), SrcPort, DstPort, Proto (IANA number, e.g. 6=TCP, 17=UDP)
- FlowDirection (0=Ingress, 1=Egress, 2=Inner), Bytes, Packets, Dscp, Flags

Packet drops (often with recordType flowLog and packetLoss dropped/hasDrops):
- PktDropPackets, PktDropBytes, PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsId, DnsLatencyMs, DnsErrno, DnsFlagsResponseCode

Examples:
- SrcK8S_Namespace=openshift-netobserv&SrcK8S_Name~my-app
- Proto=6&DstPort=443
- SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b

tools.name: netobserv_get_flow_metrics
tools.description: Returns aggregated NetObserv flow metrics as topology or time-series data. Use for throughput, TLS/DNS/drop breakdowns, and namespace or workload traffic analysis; see aggregateBy and groups for grouping options.

aggregateBy.description:
Primary dimension for netobserv_get_flow_metrics (console plugin /api/flow/metrics).

Two forms (use exact spelling):

1) Topology scopes — aggregate endpoints for graph/topology views:
- app — application workloads (pods/services), excluding infrastructure traffic
- namespace — Kubernetes namespace (default)
- owner — controller owner (Deployment, StatefulSet, …)
- resource — pod, service, or node (finest workload granularity)
- host — node name
- zone — availability zone
- cluster — cluster name (multi-cluster)
- network — user-defined / secondary network name

2) Flow record fields — group by a single flow attribute (PascalCase field name).
Use for breakdown charts (TLS, DNS, drops, protocol). Field names match filters / flow logs.

TLS (requires TLS tracking on the FlowCollector):
- TLSVersion, TLSCipherSuite, TLSGroup, TLSTypes

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsFlagsResponseCode, DnsErrno

Packet drops:
- PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

Network / K8s (single-sided breakdown; pair with filters for src/dst):
- Proto, SrcPort, DstPort, FlowDirection, Dscp
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type, SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone
- K8S_ClusterName, SrcK8S_NetworkName, DstK8S_NetworkName

Pair aggregateBy with type and function:
- Throughput: type=Bytes or Packets, function=rate
- Flow count: type=Flows, function=count or rate
- DNS volume: type=DnsFlows, function=count
- DNS latency: type=DnsLatencyMs, function=avg, p90, or max
- RTT: type=TimeFlowRttNs, function=avg, min, or p90
- Drops: type=PktDropPackets or PktDropBytes, function=rate

Examples:
- aggregateBy=namespace, type=Bytes, function=rate
- aggregateBy=TLSVersion, type=Bytes, function=rate, filters=TLSTypes!~""
- aggregateBy=TLSGroup, type=Flows, function=count
- aggregateBy=DnsFlagsResponseCode, type=DnsFlows, function=count
- aggregateBy=PktDropLatestState, type=PktDropPackets, function=rate, packetLoss=dropped
- aggregateBy=resource, type=Bytes, function=rate, namespace=netobserv

- Deployed canary: engine-v2-1 (2 replicas) using quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29, matching the stable deployment’s container name, containerPort (80), and security configuration.

Current state:
- Stable: engine-v2-0 — 2 pods Running
- Canary: engine-v2-1 — 2 pods Running
- Service: recommendation-engine — selects app=recommendation-engine (both deployments)

How to validate quickly:
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get pods -l app=recommendation-engine -o wide
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
- Send traffic to the Service (ClusterIP/port 80) and observe that it hits both sets of pods approximately evenly.

Adjust/rollback:
- To revert to 100% stable: update the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.
- To bias traffic without a mesh/ingress splitter: adjust replica counts (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary ≈ 75/25).

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested a non-existent StorageClass “sc”, so the claim couldn’t bind and the pod couldn’t schedule.
- What I changed: I deleted the unbound PVC and recreated it with the existing default StorageClass “standard” (1Gi, RWO). No data loss risk since the PVC was never bound.

Current state:
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) via StorageClass standard
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster (container nginx is ready)

If you intended a different StorageClass (available: csi-hostpath-sc, standard), or need a different size/access mode, tell me and I’ll adjust.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I fixed it.

- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested a non-existent StorageClass “sc”, so the claim couldn’t bind and the pod couldn’t schedule.
- What I changed: I deleted the unbound PVC and recreated it with the existing default StorageClass “standard” (1Gi, RWO). No data loss risk since the PVC was never bound.

Current state:
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) via StorageClass standard
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster (container nginx is ready)

If you intended a different StorageClass (available: csi-hostpath-sc, standard), or need a different size/access mode, tell me and I’ll adjust.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested a non-existent StorageClass “sc”, so the claim couldn’t bind and the pod couldn’t schedule.
- What I changed: I deleted the unbound PVC and recreated it with the existing default StorageClass “standard” (1Gi, RWO). No data loss risk since the PVC was never bound.

Current state:
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) via StorageClass standard
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster (container nginx is ready)

If you intended a different StorageClass (available: csi-hostpath-sc, standard), or need a different size/access mode, tell me and I’ll adjust.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080, but the liveness/readiness probes were checking port 80 on paths /get_status and /is_ready. That caused probe failures and the pod never became Ready.
- The Service was targeting port 80, so even if the pod was up, traffic would hit the wrong port.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment’s health checks to GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service still listens on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod orders/webapp-5fb688dc88-rzw47: 1/1 Running and Ready.
- Service orders/webapp Endpoints: 10.244.0.25:8080.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/
- Or: kubectl -n orders port-forward deploy/webapp 8080:8080 and open http://localhost:8080

If you need external access (Ingress/LoadBalancer), tell me the hostname or exposure type you want and I’ll set it up. If you intended to keep custom health endpoints (/get_status, /is_ready), I can configure nginx to serve those instead.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080, but the liveness/readiness probes were checking port 80 on paths /get_status and /is_ready. That caused probe failures and the pod never became Ready.
- The Service was targeting port 80, so even if the pod was up, traffic would hit the wrong port.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment’s health checks to GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service still listens on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod orders/webapp-5fb688dc88-rzw47: 1/1 Running and Ready.
- Service orders/webapp Endpoints: 10.244.0.25:8080.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/
- Or: kubectl -n orders port-forward deploy/webapp 8080:8080 and open http://localhost:8080

If you need external access (Ingress/LoadBalancer), tell me the hostname or exposure type you want and I’ll set it up. If you intended to keep custom health endpoints (/get_status, /is_ready), I can configure nginx to serve those instead.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080, but the liveness/readiness probes were checking port 80 on paths /get_status and /is_ready. That caused probe failures and the pod never became Ready.
- The Service was targeting port 80, so even if the pod was up, traffic would hit the wrong port.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment’s health checks to GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service still listens on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod orders/webapp-5fb688dc88-rzw47: 1/1 Running and Ready.
- Service orders/webapp Endpoints: 10.244.0.25:8080.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/
- Or: kubectl -n orders port-forward deploy/webapp 8080:8080 and open http://localhost:8080

If you need external access (Ingress/LoadBalancer), tell me the hostname or exposure type you want and I’ll set it up. If you intended to keep custom health endpoints (/get_status, /is_ready), I can configure nginx to serve those instead.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account didn’t grant permission on pods. It only allowed list on apps/deployments.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account didn’t grant permission on pods. It only allowed list on apps/deployments.
- The RoleBinding was correct (simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader -> Role/pod-reader-role), but the Role itself lacked "pods" rules.

What I fixed
- Updated Role pod-reader-role in simple-rbac-setup to include permission to list core/v1 pods.
  - Added rule: apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["list"]
  - Kept existing apps/deployments list rule.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup get pods

Optional
- If you also want to watch or get pod details, I can add verbs ["get","watch"].
- For other actions (logs, exec, port-forward), separate permissions are needed.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels.
  - Service nginx (type ClusterIP) had selector app=web.
  - The Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so traffic to the Service IP/ DNS went nowhere.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Pods:
  - selector: app: nginx
  - targetPort remains 8080 (correct for nginx-unprivileged image that listens on 8080).

Verification
- Endpoints now populated: web/nginx -> 10.244.0.26:8080.
- From a test pod in the same namespace, curl http://nginx returns the nginx index.html.

Current state
- nginx Service is accessible inside the cluster via:
  - DNS: http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local (or just http://nginx from web namespace)
  - ClusterIP: http://10.106.151.102

If you need external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (internal only). To reach it from outside the cluster, choose one:
  - NodePort:
    kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
  - LoadBalancer (if your cluster supports it):
    kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'
  - Ingress/Route: create an Ingress pointing to svc/nginx port 80.

Would you like me to clean up the temporary curltest/nettest pods or expose the Service externally for you?

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels.
  - Service nginx (type ClusterIP) had selector app=web.
  - The Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so traffic to the Service IP/ DNS went nowhere.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Pods:
  - selector: app: nginx
  - targetPort remains 8080 (correct for nginx-unprivileged image that listens on 8080).

Verification
- Endpoints now populated: web/nginx -> 10.244.0.26:8080.
- From a test pod in the same namespace, curl http://nginx returns the nginx index.html.

Current state
- nginx Service is accessible inside the cluster via:
  - DNS: http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local (or just http://nginx from web namespace)
  - ClusterIP: http://10.106.151.102

If you need external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (internal only). To reach it from outside the cluster, choose one:
  - NodePort:
    kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
  - LoadBalancer (if your cluster supports it):
    kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'
  - Ingress/Route: create an Ingress pointing to svc/nginx port 80.

Would you like me to clean up the temporary curltest/nettest pods or expose the Service externally for you?

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels.
  - Service nginx (type ClusterIP) had selector app=web.
  - The Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so traffic to the Service IP/ DNS went nowhere.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Pods:
  - selector: app: nginx
  - targetPort remains 8080 (correct for nginx-unprivileged image that listens on 8080).

Verification
- Endpoints now populated: web/nginx -> 10.244.0.26:8080.
- From a test pod in the same namespace, curl http://nginx returns the nginx index.html.

Current state
- nginx Service is accessible inside the cluster via:
  - DNS: http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local (or just http://nginx from web namespace)
  - ClusterIP: http://10.106.151.102

If you need external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (internal only). To reach it from outside the cluster, choose one:
  - NodePort:
    kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
  - LoadBalancer (if your cluster supports it):
    kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'
  - Ingress/Route: create an Ingress pointing to svc/nginx port 80.

Would you like me to clean up the temporary curltest/nettest pods or expose the Service externally for you?

results.taskOutput:
Here’s what I found and fixed.

Findings
- Pods were Pending due to an invalid nodeSelector:
  - Events: “0/1 nodes are available: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node has that label.
- After enabling scheduling, the pod failed readiness/liveness on port 80:
  - Image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 by default.
  - Readiness/liveness and Service targetPort were set to 80, causing “connection refused”.

What I changed
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Aligned ports with nginx-unprivileged:
  - Deployment: exposed containerPort 8080; readiness/liveness probes now hit port 8080.
  - Service: kept Service port at 80 (clients unchanged) and set targetPort to 8080.
- Used a rolling update (maxSurge 100%, maxUnavailable 0) to minimize disruption.

Current status
- Pods:
  - 2 replicas Running and Ready:
    - web-app-deployment-7b6b45c479-q2k4q (10.244.0.31)
    - web-app-deployment-7b6b45c479-fpq6k (10.244.0.32)
- Service/endpoints:
  - web-app-service (ClusterIP 10.97.190.199) now has 2 Ready endpoints on port 8080.
- This should resolve “connection refused” for web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local on port 80 (Service forwards to 8080).

Notes and next steps
- If you intended to run only on GPU nodes, either:
  - Add the label environment=production-gpu to the target node(s), or
  - Update the Deployment’s nodeSelector/tolerations to match your actual node labeling.
- Consider adding resource requests/limits as needed.

Let me know if you want me to validate in-cluster connectivity with a quick curl pod, or to restore a nodeSelector once nodes are properly labeled.

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Here’s what I found and fixed.

Findings
- Pods were Pending due to an invalid nodeSelector:
  - Events: “0/1 nodes are available: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node has that label.
- After enabling scheduling, the pod failed readiness/liveness on port 80:
  - Image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 by default.
  - Readiness/liveness and Service targetPort were set to 80, causing “connection refused”.

What I changed
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Aligned ports with nginx-unprivileged:
  - Deployment: exposed containerPort 8080; readiness/liveness probes now hit port 8080.
  - Service: kept Service port at 80 (clients unchanged) and set targetPort to 8080.
- Used a rolling update (maxSurge 100%, maxUnavailable 0) to minimize disruption.

Current status
- Pods:
  - 2 replicas Running and Ready:
    - web-app-deployment-7b6b45c479-q2k4q (10.244.0.31)
    - web-app-deployment-7b6b45c479-fpq6k (10.244.0.32)
- Service/endpoints:
  - web-app-service (ClusterIP 10.97.190.199) now has 2 Ready endpoints on port 8080.
- This should resolve “connection refused” for web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local on port 80 (Service forwards to 8080).

Notes and next steps
- If you intended to run only on GPU nodes, either:
  - Add the label environment=production-gpu to the target node(s), or
  - Update the Deployment’s nodeSelector/tolerations to match your actual node labeling.
- Consider adding resource requests/limits as needed.

Let me know if you want me to validate in-cluster connectivity with a quick curl pod, or to restore a nodeSelector once nodes are properly labeled.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app-deployment
  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web-app-container
          image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
          imagePullPolicy: Always
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
            initialDelaySeconds: 3
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 10
      # Removed invalid nodeSelector that prevented scheduling
      nodeSelector: {}

outputSteps.content:
Here’s what I found and fixed.

Findings
- Pods were Pending due to an invalid nodeSelector:
  - Events: “0/1 nodes are available: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node has that label.
- After enabling scheduling, the pod failed readiness/liveness on port 80:
  - Image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 by default.
  - Readiness/liveness and Service targetPort were set to 80, causing “connection refused”.

What I changed
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Aligned ports with nginx-unprivileged:
  - Deployment: exposed containerPort 8080; readiness/liveness probes now hit port 8080.
  - Service: kept Service port at 80 (clients unchanged) and set targetPort to 8080.
- Used a rolling update (maxSurge 100%, maxUnavailable 0) to minimize disruption.

Current status
- Pods:
  - 2 replicas Running and Ready:
    - web-app-deployment-7b6b45c479-q2k4q (10.244.0.31)
    - web-app-deployment-7b6b45c479-fpq6k (10.244.0.32)
- Service/endpoints:
  - web-app-service (ClusterIP 10.97.190.199) now has 2 Ready endpoints on port 8080.
- This should resolve “connection refused” for web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local on port 80 (Service forwards to 8080).

Notes and next steps
- If you intended to run only on GPU nodes, either:
  - Add the label environment=production-gpu to the target node(s), or
  - Update the Deployment’s nodeSelector/tolerations to match your actual node labeling.
- Consider adding resource requests/limits as needed.

Let me know if you want me to validate in-cluster connectivity with a quick curl pod, or to restore a nodeSelector once nodes are properly labeled.

All set. I’ve created the namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies to meet your multi-tenant dev environment requirements.

What’s in place

1) Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Per-developer access (own namespace):
  - RoleBindings grant ClusterRole=admin to each developer User and their ServiceAccount in their own namespace:
    - dev-alice: alice + alice-sa
    - dev-bob: bob + bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: charlie + charlie-sa
- Shared namespace read-only:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared grants ClusterRole=view to Users (alice, bob, charlie) and SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - No developer bindings in staging/prod; only cluster-admins can access

Note: If you prefer stricter least-privilege (prevent RBAC edits by developers), we can switch per-developer RoleBindings from ClusterRole=admin to ClusterRole=edit.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - CPU: requests 2, limits 2
  - Memory: requests 4Gi, limits 4Gi
  - Pods: 10, Services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: requests 4, limits 4
  - Memory: requests 8Gi, limits 8Gi
  - Pods: 20, Services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - CPU: requests 8, limits 8
  - Memory: requests 16Gi, limits 16Gi
  - Pods: 50, Services: 20

4) NetworkPolicies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny all (Ingress+Egress) in every non-system namespace
- Allow DNS egress (UDP/TCP 53) to kube-system/coredns in all these namespaces
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow same-namespace ingress and egress (intra-namespace communication only)
  - Allow egress to dev-shared
  - No other cross-namespace or internet egress allowed
- dev-shared:
  - Allow ingress from self and namespaces labeled env=dev
  - Allow egress to self and namespaces labeled env=dev
- staging and prod:
  - Default deny all
  - Allow same-namespace ingress and egress only
  - No dev traffic in/out (fully isolated from dev)

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented in all created namespaces; system namespaces (e.g., kube-system) are unaffected

Notes and optional next steps
- API server egress: If workloads need to talk to the Kubernetes API (https://kubernetes.default.svc:443), we can add a specific egress exception (often requires an ipBlock to control-plane IPs depending on your CNI).
- LimitRanges: To enforce per-pod/container default requests/limits (to work smoothly with the quotas), consider adding a LimitRange in each namespace.
- Access for SAs: If you want kubeconfigs/tokens for alice-sa/bob-sa/charlie-sa, I can generate secrets or ServiceAccount token projections and provide instructions.

Would you like me to:
- Switch per-developer RoleBindings from admin to edit for tighter least privilege?
- Add LimitRanges with sensible defaults?
- Add egress to the Kubernetes API server where needed?

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I’ve created the namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies to meet your multi-tenant dev environment requirements.

What’s in place

1) Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Per-developer access (own namespace):
  - RoleBindings grant ClusterRole=admin to each developer User and their ServiceAccount in their own namespace:
    - dev-alice: alice + alice-sa
    - dev-bob: bob + bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: charlie + charlie-sa
- Shared namespace read-only:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared grants ClusterRole=view to Users (alice, bob, charlie) and SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - No developer bindings in staging/prod; only cluster-admins can access

Note: If you prefer stricter least-privilege (prevent RBAC edits by developers), we can switch per-developer RoleBindings from ClusterRole=admin to ClusterRole=edit.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - CPU: requests 2, limits 2
  - Memory: requests 4Gi, limits 4Gi
  - Pods: 10, Services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: requests 4, limits 4
  - Memory: requests 8Gi, limits 8Gi
  - Pods: 20, Services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - CPU: requests 8, limits 8
  - Memory: requests 16Gi, limits 16Gi
  - Pods: 50, Services: 20

4) NetworkPolicies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny all (Ingress+Egress) in every non-system namespace
- Allow DNS egress (UDP/TCP 53) to kube-system/coredns in all these namespaces
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow same-namespace ingress and egress (intra-namespace communication only)
  - Allow egress to dev-shared
  - No other cross-namespace or internet egress allowed
- dev-shared:
  - Allow ingress from self and namespaces labeled env=dev
  - Allow egress to self and namespaces labeled env=dev
- staging and prod:
  - Default deny all
  - Allow same-namespace ingress and egress only
  - No dev traffic in/out (fully isolated from dev)

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented in all created namespaces; system namespaces (e.g., kube-system) are unaffected

Notes and optional next steps
- API server egress: If workloads need to talk to the Kubernetes API (https://kubernetes.default.svc:443), we can add a specific egress exception (often requires an ipBlock to control-plane IPs depending on your CNI).
- LimitRanges: To enforce per-pod/container default requests/limits (to work smoothly with the quotas), consider adding a LimitRange in each namespace.
- Access for SAs: If you want kubeconfigs/tokens for alice-sa/bob-sa/charlie-sa, I can generate secrets or ServiceAccount token projections and provide instructions.

Would you like me to:
- Switch per-developer RoleBindings from admin to edit for tighter least privilege?
- Add LimitRanges with sensible defaults?
- Add egress to the Kubernetes API server where needed?

outputSteps.content:
All set. I’ve created the namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies to meet your multi-tenant dev environment requirements.

What’s in place

1) Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Per-developer access (own namespace):
  - RoleBindings grant ClusterRole=admin to each developer User and their ServiceAccount in their own namespace:
    - dev-alice: alice + alice-sa
    - dev-bob: bob + bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: charlie + charlie-sa
- Shared namespace read-only:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared grants ClusterRole=view to Users (alice, bob, charlie) and SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - No developer bindings in staging/prod; only cluster-admins can access

Note: If you prefer stricter least-privilege (prevent RBAC edits by developers), we can switch per-developer RoleBindings from ClusterRole=admin to ClusterRole=edit.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - CPU: requests 2, limits 2
  - Memory: requests 4Gi, limits 4Gi
  - Pods: 10, Services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: requests 4, limits 4
  - Memory: requests 8Gi, limits 8Gi
  - Pods: 20, Services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - CPU: requests 8, limits 8
  - Memory: requests 16Gi, limits 16Gi
  - Pods: 50, Services: 20

4) NetworkPolicies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny all (Ingress+Egress) in every non-system namespace
- Allow DNS egress (UDP/TCP 53) to kube-system/coredns in all these namespaces
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow same-namespace ingress and egress (intra-namespace communication only)
  - Allow egress to dev-shared
  - No other cross-namespace or internet egress allowed
- dev-shared:
  - Allow ingress from self and namespaces labeled env=dev
  - Allow egress to self and namespaces labeled env=dev
- staging and prod:
  - Default deny all
  - Allow same-namespace ingress and egress only
  - No dev traffic in/out (fully isolated from dev)

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented in all created namespaces; system namespaces (e.g., kube-system) are unaffected

Notes and optional next steps
- API server egress: If workloads need to talk to the Kubernetes API (https://kubernetes.default.svc:443), we can add a specific egress exception (often requires an ipBlock to control-plane IPs depending on your CNI).
- LimitRanges: To enforce per-pod/container default requests/limits (to work smoothly with the quotas), consider adding a LimitRange in each namespace.
- Access for SAs: If you want kubeconfigs/tokens for alice-sa/bob-sa/charlie-sa, I can generate secrets or ServiceAccount token projections and provide instructions.

Would you like me to:
- Switch per-developer RoleBindings from admin to edit for tighter least privilege?
- Add LimitRanges with sensible defaults?
- Add egress to the Kubernetes API server where needed?
